final_message:
I've optimized the `a64_neon` variant and all work is committed. I couldn't measure any speedup: there's no AArch64 hardware here and qemu timings mean nothing. Every performance figure below is an expectation from instruction counts and an assumed model of the Cortex-X925.

**Tests:** `make -C native-kernels test-cross` reports 20/20 PASS for `a64_scalar`, `a64_neon` and `a64_sve`, and `make test` passes. I also ran several throwaway checks, not committed since only assembly belongs in the repo:
- **Guard pages:** a harness put every input and output buffer against a protected page, across many sizes, ops, data patterns and validity patterns. 0 failures.
- **Deliberate bugs:** each one I introduced into the new code was caught.
- **Block boundaries:** the chunk/block paths still pass with the size constants shrunk.
- **Registers:** a disassembly check confirms each function writes exactly the registers its comment declares and never a callee-saved one.

**What changed** (only `pq_a64_neon.S` and `pq_a64_neon.h`):
- **Comparisons:** every op except a real BETWEEN now uses one compare per 2 rows instead of two. For 128-bit rows that is 3–4 ops instead of 8. This affects filter/count for i64 and i128.
- **Mask packing and index output:** `filter_i64`, `filter_i64_bitmap` and `compare_i64` now build masks for 32 rows at a time. Writing selected row indices takes half the vector ops.
- **`minmax_i64`:** four independent accumulators remove a dependency chain that limited the loop.
- **`minmax_i128`:** a cheap test (about 13 ops per 8 rows instead of about 64) skips groups where no row can change the min or max. The exact update still runs whenever one could. On sorted or constant-hi-word data it falls back to the exact update, costing about 1–2%.
- **`group_sum_i64`:** the id check now runs per 2048-row chunk, so the ids are read from memory once (25% less memory traffic). The loop is unrolled. If a bad id appears late, the earlier chunks are subtracted back out, so the outputs end up bit-for-bit unchanged as the spec requires. Another thread reading the outputs during the call could see intermediate values.
- **`gather_i64`:** prefetches the rows 64 indices ahead.
- **Popcount and bitmap and/or/andnot:** 128 bytes per iteration, with slightly fewer ops for popcount.

**Expected effect:** the benchmark arrays (32–64 MiB) don't fit in cache, so most kernels are limited by memory bandwidth, and I don't know the target's single-core bandwidth. The README table gives each workload's expected speedup at 40 GB/s and at 80 GB/s:

| Workload | Expected speedup (40 / 80 GB/s) |
|---|---|
| `minmax_i128` | ~1.3× / ~2.6× |
| `minmax_i64` | ~1.25× / ~2× |
| `group_sum_i64` | ~1.3× / ~1.3× |
| `filter_i128` | 1.0× / ~1.7× |
| `filter_i64` | 1.0× / ~1.45× |
| `bitmap_popcount` | ~1.1× |
| `gather_i64` | 1.0–1.5× (uncertain) |
| other 10 workloads | ~1.0× |

No kernel is expected to get slower on the benchmark data.

**Limitations:**
- **Left unchanged:** I didn't touch the sum kernels, `count_i64_between`, `count_i128_between` or `hash_i64`. I judged them memory-bound. For `hash_i64`, a mixed NEON/integer version could also be slower depending on how many multiply units the core has.
- **SVE untouched:** the `a64_sve` variant is unchanged. It is the default the dispatcher picks on the X925, so normal library users won't see these gains unless they select `neon`.
- **Small inputs:** the 32-row loops leave up to 31 rows to scalar code, so those three kernels are slightly slower when n is under 64.
- **Code size:** the NEON `.text` grew from 7.5 KiB to 12.9 KiB because each comparison shape has its own loop copy.
